title: Human fraternity (2019)
hookLine: Francis and the Grand Imam of al-Azhar sign a document on fraternity in Abu Dhabi

lines: THE POPE AND THE GRAND IMAM.
cards: Two men sit at a table in Abu Dhabi, each with a pen. One is the pope, in white. The other is Ahmad al-Tayyeb, the Grand Imam of al-Azhar, the mosque and university in Cairo, in his own robes and turban.
Between them is a document neither could have signed alone. They sign it, stand, and embrace. It's called the Document on Human Fraternity for World Peace and Living Together.
Its first words name neither Rome nor Cairo. They name God.

teach.h: IN THE NAME OF GOD, ALL EQUAL.
teach.b: Read it slowly and it moves in four steps. First, the opening. It speaks in the name of God, who created all human beings equal in rights, duties and dignity, and called them to live together as brothers and sisters.
Then it names the people a phrase like that can skip over: the poor, orphans and widows, refugees, the victims of war, every human life that God forbids anyone to kill. Second, what it refuses.
Religions must never be used to incite war, hatred or violence, and God does not need to be defended by anyone killing in his name.
Two religious leaders saying that together carries a different weight from either saying it alone.

Third, what it asks for: dialogue as the path, working together as the way of acting, understanding each other as the method. Not grand words; a job description for neighbors. Fourth, what it doesn't do.
It doesn't merge two faiths, or pretend Catholics and Muslims believe the same things.
You heard the line from Assisi: together, not blended.
Catholics hear in it the Gospel's words, in the Douay-Rheims, where Jesus tells his followers: "one is your master; and all you are brethren." Muslims bring their own scripture and their own reasons.
Both men signed in their own names, from their own traditions. And the two signers asked that it be studied in schools, universities and places of formation, so the young would meet it close to home.

how: Catholic dioceses and parishes take part in interreligious dialogue with local mosques and Muslim communities, sharing meals, joint service projects and study, and some mark the International Day of Human Fraternity, set by the United Nations on the anniversary of the signing.

games.q: the pope and the Grand Imam have signed their document. how should people meet it?

practice: Picture a Muslim you know or see often, a coworker, a shopkeeper, a parent at the school gate, or, if no one comes, any neighbor you've never really greeted.

Imagine saying hello properly, using their name, and waiting for the answer; a common Muslim greeting means peace be upon you, and you're welcome to say it if it's natural to you. If you pray, pray for them; if not, wish them well.

wordCard.voice: Human fraternity. The document signed in Abu Dhabi by Pope Francis and the Grand Imam of al-Azhar: all people, brothers and sisters, and never violence in God's name.

orig.note: Arabic: peace be upon you, a greeting used among Muslims.

carryVoice: Your line: brothers and sisters. Two traditions at one table, neither one blended. That's day nine hundred thirty-five.
